query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel with its native (as-formed) oxide layer, exposure to harsh environments at elevated temperatures accelerates corrosion because thermal stresses induce microcracking of this protective film. This localized breakdown exposes fresh metal to aggressive species (such as Cl– ions), effectively triggering or accelerating localized galvanic corrosion. Conversely, if the oxide film remains intact, corrosion-related degradation is suppressed.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 carbon steel with its naturally formed thin oxide layer (a mixture of Fe oxides on its ferrite-pearlite microstructure).
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel samples to a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under two temperature regimes: one at room temperature (as the baseline) and the other at an elevated temperature with controlled thermal cycling (e.g., around 70°C) to induce thermal stress.
generation.conditions: Harsh, chloride-rich environment with controlled humidity; tests carried out at room temperature versus elevated temperature (with thermal cycling) to simulate service conditions. All tests are conducted under quiescent (non-flowing) conditions to isolate the effect of temperature-induced stress on the oxide film integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity (continuity and adhesion) of the native oxide (passivation) film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Differences in thermal expansion between the steel substrate and its native oxide lead to stress build‐up at elevated temperatures. This induces microcracking in the oxide layer, which compromises its protective function. The cracks expose fresh underlying metal to the electrolyte, leading to enhanced localized galvanic corrosion under the aggressive chloride environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to elevated temperature and thermal cycling will show a higher density of microcracks in the oxide film, a measurable increase in corrosion current densities, and lower polarization resistance relative to room temperature samples. Localized corrosion features (pits) will be more prevalent, indicating that corrosion rates are significantly higher compared to the untreated (room temperature) reference.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel samples kept at room temperature in the same 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, where the native oxide remains relatively intact and corrosion rates are lower.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant in steel with its unmodified native oxide layer; results may vary if the steel is pre-passivated by other means or if environmental parameters (e.g., temperature or chloride concentration) exceed the range of typical service conditions. The hypothesis assumes that minor compositional variations and surface finish are uniform across samples.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature or thermal cycling parameters at which oxide cracking becomes critical are not fully defined and may depend on subtle variations in oxide composition and microstructure. The influence of impurities or slight alloying variations in Q235 steel on oxide stability remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Q235 steel samples with identical pre-exposure conditions. Divide the samples into two groups: one immersed in 3.5 wt% NaCl at room temperature, and the other subjected to controlled thermal cycling at an elevated temperature (around 70°C) in the same solution. Use SEM and XPS to analyze the integrity and composition of the oxide layers at several time points, and perform electrochemical tests (EIS and potentiodynamic polarization) to assess corrosion kinetics.
measurements: Surface microstructure and microcrack density (via SEM)
Oxide composition and film continuity (via XPS)
Corrosion current density and polarization resistance (via potentiodynamic polarization and EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the group subjected to elevated temperature and thermal cycling does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in microcrack density, a decrease in passivation quality, or elevated corrosion current density and decreased polarization resistance relative to the room-temperature group, then the hypothesis that thermal stress-induced oxide film microcracking is the governing cause of corrosion onset is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was noted that the shape and appearance of the cracks in the aerated testing were more curved and thinner in comparison with the cracks observed in the Al-HEA coating after the exposure in the wellhead test. The effect of a difference in temperature in the aerated and the wellhead, and hence the extent of thermal stresses, could explain to some extent this variance in cracking behavior. However, no corrosion products were observed in the cracks in the Al-HEA coating, and hence the cracking was concluded to have formed due to internal stresses in the coating.
